draft.title: Managing water
card: People store and move water to meet needs. Dams hold water in reservoirs for cities, farms and power. Irrigation moves water from rivers or groundwater onto crops.
Water trading lets licence holders buy and sell water entitlements. Water can move to the users who value it most, such as a farm growing high-value crops.
Taking water changes rivers. Dams and extraction can reduce flows, change the timing of floods and harm wetlands, fish and the people who depend on them.
The Murray-Darling Basin shows competing demands. Irrigators, towns, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities and the environment all need water from the same river system.
draft.remember: Managing water means sharing a limited supply between competing uses, and every use changes the river.

a.q: Why is water use in the Murray-Darling Basin an example of competing demands?
opts: Many users need water from the same river system
Only farmers are allowed to take water from the rivers
Dams have stopped all water from flowing downstream
Water trading has ended the need for river flows
a.why: Irrigators, towns, communities and the environment all draw on the same rivers, so more for one use can mean less for another. It is wrong that only farmers take water, as the card lists several users.
a.clue: Think about who needs the same water.

b.q: Dev holds a water licence and sells part of his entitlement to a orchard grower downstream. What does this show about water trading?
opts: Water can move to a user who values it more
Water trading gives each user the same share
Water trading removes any effect on the river
Water trading is only used to fill dams
b.why: Trading lets entitlements move between users, so water can go where it is valued most. It does not give equal shares or remove effects on rivers, because the water is still taken from the river system.
b.clue: Trading changes who holds the entitlement.

a.best: Many users need water from the same river system

b.best: Water can move to a user who values it more
